I'm a Computer Scientist with a bachelors and masters. I've worked with a lot of people who don't have college degrees or minimal 2-year degrees.

There is a lot you learn in college that is more difficult to learn on your own. Things like Big-O notation, algorithms, good database design are all things I feel that University gave me a leg up on as compared to others I met without that background.

That being said, I graduated in 2004 with no debt. My parents has a college fund and I went to a state school. I got most of grad school paid for by work, and although I took out some loans, I paid them back pretty quickly. I made the mistake of moving my car onto my student loans since they were 0% while in school. After I graduated though, they went up past 6%...more than my car loan! Lucky I didn't have much.

There is a lot to get out of a 4 year degree, especially in the STEM fields. But debt will keep you trapped in that field; always feeling like you have to work forever to get out from under it. Avoid debt. Use state schools (They're about the same. You get out of any degree with you put into it. People go to MIT, do the bare minimum and I'm sure they have people who couldn't setup a web server. Some go to University of Nebraska and have their neural network projects up on github. The program is just a base to build on).

If you can avoid student loans, have your parents help and find an affordable program that you can pay for with a grocery store job, even if working full time takes you an extra year or two, graduating without debt is the best route to go.

Also: Holiday Work Visas. When you graduate, go take an internship in Australia/New Zealand. You get a 1 of working and living for free if you're under 30 (Ireland too if you've just graduated).

Don't think just about today. You've got an average of about 70 years ahead of you from today. What do you see happening? Where do you think our economy is going to be in just 20 years? Keep in mind that the automation we're seeing today hardly scratches the surface of where things are headed. Jobs with low skill requirements are already being automated away and if not automated then outsourced. And the number of potential applicants is rapidly outpacing the number of desirable jobs.

I think the broad answer to the above questions is fairly straight forward. As for the education itself, I'd suggest attending the most reputable institution you can. This isn't for prestige but because a lot of the value in a university education isn't just the education but connections and things that happen outside the classroom. Going out for weekly drinks with the guy responsible for a fundamental development in the field you're studying? That's just cool, and highly valuable had I chosen to pursue that sort of career. Depending on what you study and if you pursue research you'll also potentially be able to access facilities far beyond anything you'd have elsewhere. Being granted the right to schedule arbitrary time blocks on a multimillion dollar super computer in a digital entertainment center as part of research? Very cool.
